name: GHRP-1

lead: GHRP-1 is one of the first synthetic growth hormone releasing peptides, developed alongside GHRP-6 and GHRP-2. People look to it for higher growth hormone, which they connect to more muscle and less body fat.

It binds the ghrelin/GH secretagogue receptor, separate from the GHRH receptor, and prompts growth hormone release. A 1993 review reported that it, GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 were the three such peptides given to humans, and that all released more GH than GHRH 1-44. Studies measured hormone release; body-composition outcomes have not been tested.

paras: It is discussed in peptide and bodybuilding communities as one of the older GHRPs, usually in the context of a muscle-building or fat-loss plan. It was largely superseded by later peptides.
It is a research peptide, not an approved medicine, and little modern human safety data exists. It is prohibited in sport, and anti-doping labs have developed urine tests for it and its metabolites.

angle.text: GHRP-1 is grouped with GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 as a way to raise growth hormone for muscle gain and fat loss. It stimulates GH release through the ghrelin receptor, and some 1990s human work measured that release.

lead: GHRP-1 (growth hormone releasing peptide-1) is a synthetic peptide from the first family of growth hormone releasing peptides, which also includes GHRP-6 and GHRP-2. These small peptides of six to seven amino acids stimulate growth hormone release through a receptor distinct from the GHRH receptor.[1][2]

A 1993 review reported that GHRP-6, GHRP-1 and GHRP-2 were the three such peptides given to humans, in increasing order of effectiveness, and that all released more growth hormone than GHRH 1-44.[2] GHRP-1 is not approved as a medicine. Anti-doping laboratories have developed urine tests for it and its metabolites.[3]
No clinical trials in healthy people for appearance were found.

paras: GHRPs have no structural homology with GHRH and act at specific receptors in the pituitary and hypothalamus, later identified as the ghrelin receptor.[1][4] Wikipedia lists GHRP-1 among the synthetic agonists of this receptor.[4] Early work in animals and men also examined how prolonged GHRP infusion affects pulsatile growth hormone secretion.[5]

Human studies of GHRP-1 are from the early 1990s: reviews describe it among the peptides administered to people.[2] One phase 2 trial of a GHRP-1 formulation (GHRP-1/AG) in end-stage renal disease patients on hemodialysis was registered in 2006 and terminated with three participants.[6] Animal work on related GHRPs examined heart failure and cachexia in rats.[7]
GHRPs are on the lists of substances prohibited in sport, and analytical methods exist to detect GHRP-1 and its metabolites in urine.[3][8]

timeline.event: Review describes GHRP-6, GHRP-1 and GHRP-2 as the three GHRPs given to humans.[2]
